summary: Adds a way to send a BREAK signal over a Secure Shell terminal session. BREAK is a special attention signal from serial lines, sometimes used to get a device's console to respond. It is a standards-track extension to SSH.

plainLanguage.summary: Old computers had a special attention button on their cable. This lets you press that button from far away through a secure connection.

subtitle: How an SSH client asks the remote side to send a serial BREAK signal, as Telnet consoles already could.

tldr.problem: Console servers connect network sessions to serial ports and expect a BREAK signal, which Telnet could send but SSH could not, so users stayed on Telnet.
tldr.mechanism: A new session channel request named "break" carries a length in milliseconds, and the receiver performs a BREAK and, if asked, answers with success or failure.
tldr.outcome: SSH can now replace Telnet for console access, with advice to cap and floor the BREAK length and to restrict who may send it.

today: RFC 4335 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SSH Needs a BREAK
sections.content:
A common use of Telnet is the Console Server, which connects a Telnet session to a physical RS-232/V.24 asynchronous port so the port looks like a network-addressable device. Many vendors offer high-level administration through such a serial port and expect the attached terminal to be able to send a BREAK signal.

A BREAK is the TxD signal held in a SPACE ("0") state for longer than a whole character time, typically 250 to 500 ms. Telnet (RFC 854) has a way to send one, and console server vendors treat it as a physical BREAK. SSH had no equivalent, which kept users on Telnet for this job.
sections.plainLanguage: Some machines have a special "wake up!" signal you send down the cable. Telnet could send it, but the secure option could not, so people kept using the unsafe one.

sections.title: The Break Request
sections.content:
The extension is a channel-specific request sent over an SSH session channel. Its fields are: a byte SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_REQUEST, a uint32 recipient channel, the string "break", a boolean want_reply, and a uint32 break-length in milliseconds.

If the want_reply flag is set, the server MUST answer with SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_SUCCESS if a BREAK of any kind was performed, or SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_FAILURE if none was. The RFC says this operation SHOULD be supported by any general purpose SSH client.
sections.plainLanguage: The message says "please send the wake-up signal for this many milliseconds," and can ask for a yes or no answer back.

sections.title: Break Length Rules
sections.content:
If the receiving application cannot control the BREAK length, it SHOULD ignore the length parameter and send the default BREAK of the chipset or its driver.

If it can control the length, the RFC suggests:

  • A request above 3000 ms SHOULD be treated as 3000 ms. This avoids a port being tied up for as long as 49.7 days.
  • A request below 500 ms SHOULD be treated as 500 ms, since most devices recognize a BREAK of that length.
  • A length of 0 SHOULD mean the default BREAK of the chipset or driver, and if there is no default, 500 ms can be used.

Applications that need a longer or shorter BREAK may choose to ignore these suggestions.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone asks for an absurdly long beep, you cut it short. If the beep is too quick for anyone to notice, you stretch it a bit.

sections.title: Non-Serial and Cascaded Connections
sections.content:
If the SSH connection does not end at a physical serial port, the BREAK indication SHOULD be handled in a way consistent with BREAK's general use as an attention or interrupt signal. The RFC's example is a service processor that needs an out-of-band way to get the attention of a system it manages.

When an SSH connection cascades into another connection, the BREAK SHOULD be passed along. A Telnet session started from an SSH shell should carry an SSH-initiated BREAK, and an SSH client started from a Telnet connection SHOULD pass on a BREAK indication from the Telnet side.
sections.plainLanguage: If the message goes through several helpers, each one should pass the wake-up signal along to the next.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Many systems treat serial consoles as local and secured, and a BREAK can halt the operating system or open privileged configuration modes. Access to BREAK-enabled ports over SSH should therefore be limited to users with suitable privileges. Alternatively, BREAK support MAY be configurable per port or per server.

An implementation that follows the length parameter literally, without the suggested time limit, may cause a denial of service or unexpected results on attached devices that receive a very long BREAK.

IANA has assigned the Connection Protocol Channel Request Name break.
sections.plainLanguage: The wake-up signal can be powerful, so only trusted people should be allowed to send it, and it should not be allowed to go on forever.
